citations.quote:
**(a) Adopted readings and framework data.** Adopt the state and composition
postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable
and probability postulate
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2), the
autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]]
(P4) and the preparation and apparatus postulate
[[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]] (P7), together with the
Boltzmann-constant and temperature conventions of
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]]. Declare one of the
following model readings of the same **adopted Gibbs assignment**:

(i) a fixed-$N$ model of
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-declared-fixed-n-model]], on its sector space,
with Gibbs generator $G:=H_N^\sigma$; or

(ii) a separately declared number-variable mode model, such as a one-mode
bosonic Fock space, a fermionic occupation space, or a declared countable
independent-mode space, with its declared assigned observables and energy
operator $H$. The model declares a self-adjoint Gibbs generator $G$ on that
space: either $G=H$, or a separately supplied self-adjoint realization of the
effective generator $G=H-\mu\mathcal N$, where $\mathcal N$ is the declared
particle-number operator and $\mu\in\mathbb R$ is an assigned chemical
potential in joules. The subtraction is an operator with its supplied domain,
not an assertion that a formal unbounded difference is self-adjoint.

In either reading assume $G$ is bounded below and give its spectral PVM
$E_G$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Let $T>0$ be an assigned temperature in
kelvin and let $\beta:=1/(k_BT)$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$ with the assigned
Boltzmann constant $k_B$. The Gibbs assignment to either model, and the
chemical-potential identification in (ii), are additional physical
preparation assumptions made here; they are not derived from P1-P4 or from
the fixed-$N$ construction. In (ii) no restriction on the assigned real
$\mu$ is imposed beyond the declared generator and trace existence
conditions; the mode-specific convergence conditions are proved separately.
For reading (ii), $G$ specifies the Gibbs weights. If the assigned autonomous
dynamics is generated by $H$, stationarity of the Gibbs density requires its
separate dynamical or commutation hypotheses; this assignment does not
identify $H-\mu\mathcal N$ with the physical evolution generator.
The physical Helmholtz free-energy vocabulary of the entropy definition
continues to apply only to its stated nonzero finite-sector class and is not
extended to every effective generator by this postulate.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of
the spectral calculus.

**(b) Existence hypothesis and the Gibbs preparation.** The model assumes
that the **partition trace is strictly positive and finite**:
$$0<Z:=\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta G}<\infty,$$
where $\operatorname{Tr}B:=\sum_{f\in\mathcal B}\langle Bf,f\rangle$ for a
bounded positive $B$ and an orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$, with value allowed
to be $+\infty$. Such a basis exists under the declared AC by the maximal
orthonormal-family argument using [[thm-zorn]] and the zero-complement
criterion of [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]].
This trace is basis independent: for $C:=B^{1/2}$ of
[[thm-positive-square-root]], the defining sum is
$\sum_{f\in\mathcal B}\|Cf\|^2$, whose invariance is
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. When the sum is finite,
$C$ is Hilbert-Schmidt ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), so $B=C^2$ is
trace class by [[thm-trace-class-iff-product-of-two-hilbert-schmidt-operators]],
and its ordinary trace is this same diagonal sum by
[[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]. Apply this to the bounded positive operator $e^{-\beta G}$, since the
declared Gibbs generator $G$ is bounded below. The model
adopts as the **canonical** or **Gibbs preparation** of the declared model
at temperature $T$ the density operator
$$\rho_\beta:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta G}.$$
If the sector is zero-dimensional, its partition trace is $Z=0$, no
trace-one density exists, and no canonical density or equilibrium free
energy is assigned. On a nonzero finite-dimensional model space, $Z$ is a
positive finite sum $\sum_je^{-\beta E_j}$ over the eigenvalues of $G$; no energy
sign restriction is needed. There $\rho_\beta$ is the canonical operator of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-finite-gibbs-free-energy-minimum]], and the
strict positivity and finiteness hypothesis is automatic. In reading (i),
$Z=Z_N$ and this is precisely the finite-sector Gibbs assignment.

Outside the finite-dimensional class the existence hypothesis is a genuine
restriction. For a declared non-interacting fixed-$N$ model with a supplied
countably infinite orthonormal eigenmode basis and real mode energies
$\varepsilon_j$ bounded below, the complete construction and trace criterion
of [[lem-nrqm-many-body-fixed-n-countable-mode-partition-criterion]] give
$Z_N=h_N(q)$ for bosonic statistics or $Z_N=e_N(q)$ for fermionic statistics,
where $q_j=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}$ and $h_N,e_N$ are the corresponding
nonnegative occupation-series sums. For every fixed $N\ge1$, either trace is
finite exactly when $\sum_jq_j<\infty$. This is a trace on the fixed-$N$
sector and permits negative mode energies.

For the separately declared full bosonic Fock models of reading (ii),
the single-mode calculation of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-single-mode-thermal-trace]] and the product
criterion of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-countable-mode-product-criterion]]
provide the separate mathematical full-Fock traces, with their original
positive mode-energy hypotheses: they sum over every particle number,
including the vacuum, giving $(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon})^{-1}$ for one mode
and $\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j})^{-1}$ for countably many modes.
Their physical Gibbs reading is the additional assignment of (a)(ii), not a
consequence of a mathematical trace formula. Those full-Fock traces are not
substituted for the fixed-$N$ partition trace of reading (i).

**(c) The equilibrium assumption and thermal means.** The model **assumes**
that, for a declared sample of the species at the assigned temperature $T$
and in the absence of further preparation information, the preparation
description of the sample is $\rho_\beta$ in the sense of P1. For an assigned
sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, define its outcome law
$\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta E_A(B))$ as in
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b).
If and only if the absolute first moment is finite,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|a|\,d\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(a)<\infty,$$
the model defines the **thermal mean** at temperature $T$ by
$$\langle A\rangle_\beta:=\int_{\mathbb R}a\,d\mu_{\rho_\beta}^A(a),$$
read in the assigned unit $u_A$. For bounded $A$ this equals
$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta A)=\operatorname{tr}(A\rho_\beta)$. For
unbounded $A$, if the mean exists and the literal product $A\rho_\beta$ is
defined on the whole Hilbert space and is trace class, the mean also equals
$\operatorname{tr}(A\rho_\beta)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(\overline{\rho_\beta A})$; these conditional product
identities are proved by the density eigenexpansion in
[[lem-nrqm-many-body-spectral-mean-and-defined-trace-product]]. First-moment
existence alone imposes no such product or operator-square-domain condition.
When the absolute first moment is infinite the model asserts no finite
thermal mean. The identification of the parameter $T$ with the thermodynamic temperature of a
sample, and of $\beta$ with its inverse temperature, is part of this
assumption; the stated conservation and equilibrium properties of
$\rho_\beta$ under the flow of P4, and the extremal property of $\rho_\beta$
among preparations, are separate conditional results of this pair.

**(d) Motivation and status.** The assumption is motivated, but not
established, by the maximum-entropy reasoning of the cited sources: among
preparations with a prescribed mean energy, the Gibbs weights maximize the
entropy functional, and the finite-dimensional comparison theorem makes
$\rho_\beta$ the minimizer of the corresponding functional built from $G$.
Its physical Helmholtz free-energy reading applies in the stated finite
fixed-sector class; an effective-generator interpretation in a different
mode model is a separate declared reading. That reasoning is
an argument inside mathematical statistics and thermodynamics; it does not
derive the physical assumption that a sample is described by $\rho_\beta$.
The postulate is an **adopted** statistical-mechanical assumption of the
model, in the sense of the content model's distinction between adopted
assumptions and derived consequences.

**(e) Scope.** The postulate asserts nothing about how a sample reaches the
Gibbs preparation; in particular it asserts no thermalization, no equilibration
time, no ergodicity, no master-equation or Markov approximation, no
thermodynamic limit, no pressure, volume or phase-transition structure, and
no measured temperature or expectation. The requirement $0<Z<\infty$ is part
of the assumption; the model does not define a canonical preparation when
$Z=0$ or the partition trace diverges. Any comparison with a laboratory sample requires the
declared preparation, isolation, detection and sampling models of P7, and
agreement of a thermal prediction with data is evidence about the combined
model and apparatus assumptions, not a proof of the framework or of this
postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\omega>0$ and
$\beta>0$ be real parameters, let $F(\mathbb C)$ be the one-mode Fock space
with its complete orthonormal family $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ and number
operator $N$ as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fixed-mode-number-law]]
and [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-number-operator-domain]], and define the
operator $G_\beta\in\mathcal B(F(\mathbb C))$ by
$$G_\beta e_n:=e^{-\beta\omega n}e_n\qquad(n\in\mathbb N)$$
together with bounded linear extension. Then:

(a) $G_\beta$ is a bounded self-adjoint positive operator with $\|G_\beta\|=1$,
and $G_\beta=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb N}e^{-\beta\omega n}\,\mathrm{id}$ on the
Fock sectors ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]);

(b) the series of weights converge,
$$Z(\beta):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}e^{-\beta\omega n}=\frac1{1-e^{-\beta\omega}},\qquad \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}n\,e^{-\beta\omega n}=\frac{e^{-\beta\omega}}{(1-e^{-\beta\omega})^2};$$

(c) $G_\beta$ is trace class with
$\|G_\beta\|_1=\operatorname{tr}G_\beta=Z(\beta)$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);

(d) $\rho_\beta:=G_\beta/Z(\beta)$ is a density operator on $F(\mathbb C)$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]), and its
number expectation, defined by the absolutely convergent spectral sum
$\langle N\rangle_\beta:=\sum_{n}n\,e^{-\beta\omega n}/Z(\beta)$, equals
$$\langle N\rangle_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta\omega}}{1-e^{-\beta\omega}}=\frac1{e^{\beta\omega}-1};$$
more generally $\sum_nn^k e^{-\beta\omega n}<\infty$ for every $k\ge1$.

The parameter $\beta$ is a positive real parameter of the model; its
identification with an inverse temperature, and the interpretation of
$\rho_\beta$ as a physical thermal state, are additional physical assumptions
not asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\varepsilon>0$ and $\beta>0$ be real parameters, let $\mathfrak h$ be a
two-dimensional complex Hilbert space with orthonormal basis
$(u_0,u_1)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
and let $H:=T_{u_1,u_1}\varepsilon=\varepsilon\,T_{u_1,u_1}$ be the
self-adjoint operator with eigenvalues $0$ on $\mathbb Cu_0$ and
$\varepsilon$ on $\mathbb Cu_1$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]). Let
$$Z:=\sum_{j=0}^{1}e^{-\beta E_j},\qquad \rho_\beta:=\frac1Z\sum_{j=0}^{1}e^{-\beta E_j}T_{u_j,u_j},\qquad s(\rho):=-\sum_{i:\,w_i>0}w_i\log w_i$$
be the partition sum, canonical operator and entropy of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-finite-gibbs-free-energy-minimum]] clause
(a), with $E_0=0$, $E_1=\varepsilon$ and $w_i$ the eigenvalues of a density
operator $\rho$ on $\mathfrak h$ ([[def-natural-logarithm]]). Then:

(a) $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}\in(1,2)$, and
$$\rho_\beta=\frac1Z\bigl(T_{u_0,u_0}+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}T_{u_1,u_1}\bigr)$$
is a density operator on $\mathfrak h$ that is not the maximally mixed state
$\tfrac12\mathrm{id}$;

(b) the mean energy is the exact identity
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\frac{\varepsilon e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}{Z}=\frac{\varepsilon}{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1},\qquad 0<\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)<\frac{\varepsilon}{2};$$

(c) the entropy and free energy satisfy
$$s(\rho_\beta)=\log Z+\frac{\beta\varepsilon}{e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1}=\log\bigl(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}\bigr)+\frac{\beta\varepsilon\,e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}{1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}},\qquad 0\le s(\rho_\beta)<\log 2,$$
and, with $F:=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=F ;$$

(d) *scope*: clauses (a)-(c) are exact algebraic identities for the
declared two-dimensional Hilbert space and the two real parameters
$\varepsilon,\beta>0$; no temperature, thermodynamic, equilibrium or
measurement interpretation is asserted, and the parameter $\beta$ carries no
physical dimension in this lemma.

Adopt the canonical equilibrium-ensemble postulate
[[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] for the mode models
declared below, the state and probability postulates P1, P2
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]]) in the readings of
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] and
[[pthm-nrqm-observables-preparation-moments]], and the
identical-particle and spin postulate P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]); assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Temperatures are assigned as in
[[def-nrqm-many-body-framework-entropy-and-free-energy]], so that
$\beta=1/(k_BT)$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$. Declare the occupation readouts as assigned sharp observables $(N,1)$ and $(N_-,1)$, with unit particle-count, which is dimensionless. The total particle-number operator $\mathcal N$ in the countable-mode reading has the same unit; every occupation mean and higher number moment below is read in the corresponding dimensionless count unit. Then:

(a) *single bosonic mode*: let $F(\mathbb C)$ be the one-mode Fock space with
number operator $N$ and orthonormal number basis $(e_n)$
([[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fixed-mode-number-law]],
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-number-operator-domain]]), let
$\varepsilon>0$ and let the model declare the energy operator $H:=\varepsilon N$
on $F(\mathbb C)$; the model's canonical preparation at temperature $T$ is
$\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta H}/Z$ with $Z=(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon})^{-1}$, the
number readout $N$ is an assigned sharp observable with finite thermal mean
$$\langle N\rangle_\beta=\frac1{e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1}=\frac1{e^{\varepsilon/(k_BT)}-1},$$
and all moments $\langle N^k\rangle_\beta$, $k\ge1$, are finite;

(b) *single fermionic orbital and grand-canonical shift*: on
$\mathfrak h=\mathbb C^2$ with occupation operator $N_-$ and
$\varepsilon_1,\mu\in\mathbb R$, the model's canonical (grand-canonical)
preparation $F=Z^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^1e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)k}T_{u_k,u_k}$
has $Z=1+e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}$, $\operatorname{tr}F=1$, and occupation mean
$$\langle N_-\rangle=\frac1{e^{\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}+1};$$
the same formula is the model's thermal mean when $\mu=0$ and
$\varepsilon_1>0$;

(c) *countably many independent modes*: let $(\varepsilon_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq(0,\infty)$
and $\mu\in\mathbb R$, and let the model declare the free-mode energies
$\varepsilon_j$ (one mode case of clause (a)) with the product reading of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-countable-mode-product-criterion]]; then the
bosonic product partition is finite exactly when
$\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$ and $\mu<\inf_j\varepsilon_j$, and
the fermionic product partition is finite exactly when
$\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$; in the finite cases the products
equal $\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_j-\mu)})^{-1}$ and
$\prod_j(1+e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_j-\mu)})$ respectively;

(d) *dilute remainders*: for $q=e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}$ the model's
occupation means satisfy the exact identities
$$\frac q{1-q}=q+\frac{q^2}{1-q}\quad(\text{bosonic},\ 0<q<1),\qquad \frac q{1+q}=q-\frac{q^2}{1+q}\quad(\text{fermionic},\ q>0),$$
so both differ from $q$ by at most $q^2/(1-q)$ and $q^2/(1+q)$
respectively;

(e) *scope*: clauses (a)-(d) are conditional statements about the declared
mode models together with the adopted ensemble assignment; they assert no
thermodynamic limit, no continuum of radiation modes, no Bose-Einstein
condensation, no measured occupation number, and no thermalisation of a
sample. All numerical equalities are exact identities of the declared
finite-mode (or product) models at the assigned temperature.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Q^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Q$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. For a rational power $q$, dimension powers mean $[X]^q=\ell^{qa}\tau^{qb}\mu^{qc}\vartheta^{qd}$ when $[X]=\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$. Rational exponents include the half-integer wave-function dimensions in clause (d); the integer-exponent dimensions form the subgroup $\mathbb Z^4$. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

For extensions using temperature, adjoin an independent dimension symbol $\Theta$: the enlarged group is $\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q$, written $\ell^a\tau^b\mu^c\vartheta^d\Theta^e$, with the same componentwise rules. The preceding group embeds by $e=0$, so all previously assigned dimensions are preserved. Temperature has dimension $\Theta$, the Boltzmann constant has dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}\Theta^{-1}$, and entropy in joules per kelvin has that same dimension; a dimensionless entropy remains dimensionless. This convention does not assign a temperature or an entropy to any system.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. In the temperature extension the reference unit of $\Theta$ is the kelvin (K), so the general reference unit gains a factor $\mathrm K^e$.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. These are real scalar constants with dimensions and units $[h]=[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (J s), $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (m s$^{-1}$), and $[e]=\vartheta$ (C). The vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is a positive real scalar that is experimentally determined in the current SI, with $[\mu_{0}]=\mu\ell\vartheta^{-2}$ (N A$^{-2}$ = H m$^{-1}$); $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$ is a positive real scalar with $[\varepsilon_{0}]=\mu^{-1}\ell^{-3}\tau^{2}\vartheta^{2}$ (F m$^{-1}$). These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: in the ordinary continuous-field regime, fix an integer $d\ge1$, an open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. A **probability current density** is a declared continuous map $j:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^d$, whose spatial components have dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$ and reference unit $\mathrm m^{1-d}\mathrm s^{-1}$. At fixed time it is a spatial vector field; its signed normal component is read as probability transported per unit spatial $(d-1)$-area and time. Explicitly, for a flat face $S=\{x:x_k=a,\ a_i\le x_i\le b_i\ (i\ne k)\}\subset\Omega$, with $a_i<b_i$ and chosen normal $n=\epsilon e_k$, $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, define its **signed probability flux** at $t\in I$ as $\Phi_S(t):=\epsilon\int_{\prod_{i\ne k}[a_i,b_i]}j_k(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},a,x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d,t)\prod_{i\ne k}dx_i$. Here $e_k$ is the $k$th coordinate unit vector and the integral uses $(d-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure; for $d=1$ this means $\Phi_{\{a\}}(t)=\epsilon j(a,t)$. The flux has dimension $\tau^{-1}$ and unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$; positive sign means transport in the chosen normal direction. Fluxes through curved surfaces, or currents with weaker regularity, require separately specified surface measures or traces. This fixes the quantity type and flux convention; it supplies neither a current associated to an arbitrary $L^2$ state nor a conservation or detector law. Each dynamical model supplies its current construction and balance hypotheses.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$. A countable probability law on $I$ means a nonnegative family with total sum $1$ under the finite-subsum convention above; these weights form such a law because $\sum_i p_i(\beta)=Z(\beta)/Z(\beta)=1$. For any real family $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

derivations.claim: For one bosonic mode, [F2] gives $Z_B=(1-q)^{-1}$ and $\langle N\rangle_B=q/(1-q)$; for $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$, multiplication of numerator and denominator by $e^{\beta\varepsilon}$ gives $q/(1-q)=1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}-1)$. The unit convention in [F6] makes the exponent dimensionless.
For one fermionic occupation, [F3] gives $Z_F=1+q$ and upper-level probability $q/(1+q)$; multiplying numerator and denominator by $e^{\beta\varepsilon}$ gives $q/(1+q)=1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)$.

For the finite product model of the Statement, the diagonal Gibbs operator satisfies $K_\beta u_{\mathbf n}=e^{-\beta E(\mathbf n)}u_{\mathbf n}=\prod_{r=1}^m q_r^{n_r}u_{\mathbf n}$, where $q_r=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_r}$. For $N\ge1$ let $C_{r,N}=\{0,\ldots,N\}$ for a bosonic factor and $C_{r,N}=\{0,1\}$ for a fermionic factor, and put $C_N=\prod_rC_{r,N}$. These are finite increasing sets whose union is $\mathcal C$. Finite distributivity gives $\sum_{\mathbf n\in C_N}\prod_rq_r^{n_r}=\prod_r\sum_{n_r\in C_{r,N}}q_r^{n_r}$. By the positive-basis trace convention in [F1] and the nonnegative-sum convention [F7], the full trace is the supremum of its finite subsums; every finite subset of $\mathcal C$ is contained in some $C_N$. Hence $0<Z=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{\mathbf n\in C_N}\prod_rq_r^{n_r}=\prod_{r=1}^m Z_r<\infty$, where $Z_r=Z_B$ or $Z_F$ from steps 1.1–1.2. Clause (b) of [F1] now makes $K_\beta$ trace class and licenses $\rho_\beta=K_\beta/Z$. The assigned label readout has singleton projection $Q(\{\mathbf n\})\psi=\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle u_{\mathbf n}$, so clause (c) gives $P(\mathbf n)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta Q(\{\mathbf n\}))=e^{-\beta E(\mathbf n)}/Z=\prod_r(q_r^{n_r}/Z_r)$. For fixed factor $s$ and occupation $k\in\mathcal C_s$, summing over the other labels in $C_N$ with $n_s=k$ gives $(q_s^k/Z)\prod_{r\ne s}\sum_{n_r\in C_{r,N}}q_r^{n_r}$ once $N\ge k$; taking $N\to\infty$ and using $Z=\prod_rZ_r$ yields the marginal $P_s(k)=q_s^k/Z_s$. The marginal is the law of the assigned $\mathcal N_s$, and its absolute first moment is finite by the bosonic first-moment sum in [F2] or the finite two-level sum in [F3]. Thus its thermal mean is the corresponding one-mode mean in steps 1.1–1.2.

Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove the one-mode factors, and step 2.1 proves trace factorization and all marginal means for the declared finite product model. These are conditional model calculations under the adopted Gibbs preparation.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Assume AC and Countable Choice and adopt the quantum Gibbs preparation of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] at assigned temperature $T>0$ kelvins, with $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. A finite independent mode list means an integer $m\ge1$ and, for each $r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, a declared type B or F and an excitation energy $\varepsilon_r>0$ joules. For type B take the one-mode Fock Hilbert space with complete number basis $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ and self-adjoint occupation operator $N_re_n=ne_n$ on its exact diagonal domain as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-single-mode-thermal-trace]]. For type F take $\mathcal H_r=\mathbb C^2$ with orthonormal basis $f_0,f_1$ and $N_rf_n=nf_n$. In either case put $H_r=\varepsilon_rN_r$, and write $u_{r,n}=e_n$ or $f_n$ according to the factor type. Define $\mathcal H^{(1)}=\mathcal H_1$ and recursively $\mathcal H^{(r+1)}=\mathcal H^{(r)}\widehat\otimes\mathcal H_{r+1}$ by the completed Hilbert tensor construction of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]; let $\mathcal H=\mathcal H^{(m)}$. The canonical orthonormal product basis is $u_{\mathbf n}=\bigotimes_r u_{r,n_r}$, indexed by $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_m)\in\mathcal C:=\prod_r\mathcal C_r$, where $\mathcal C_r=\mathbb N_0$ for type B and $\mathcal C_r=\{0,1\}$ for type F. If all factors are F then $\mathcal C$ is finite; otherwise it is countably infinite and is enumerated by increasing $\sum_r n_r$ and lexicographic order within each finite level, which is finite because every $n_r\le\sum_r n_r$. For each factor put $\hat\varepsilon_r=\varepsilon_r/(1\,\mathrm J)$. Define the numerical energy map $\hat E:\mathcal C\to\mathbb R$ by $\hat E(\mathbf n)=\sum_{r=1}^m\hat\varepsilon_rn_r$ and the physical energy $E(\mathbf n)=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat E(\mathbf n)$. Define the numerical self-adjoint diagonal operator $\hat H$ by $\hat Hu_{\mathbf n}=\hat E(\mathbf n)u_{\mathbf n}$ on the exact domain
$$D(\hat H)=\Bigl\{\psi\in\mathcal H:\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathcal C}\hat E(\mathbf n)^2|\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\};$$
when $\mathcal C$ is finite, $\hat H$ is a finite real diagonal endomorphism and is self-adjoint; when $\mathcal C$ is countably infinite, the diagonal-operator lemma [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] gives $\hat H$ self-adjoint for the displayed enumeration. The physical total energy operator is $H=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat H$, with $Hu_{\mathbf n}=E(\mathbf n)u_{\mathbf n}$ and $D(H)=D(\hat H)$; multiplication by a nonzero real scalar preserves self-adjointness.
This sum-energy Hamiltonian with no interaction term is the definition of independence for this quantum model.

Assign each factor readout $(N_r,1)$ and the composite readout $(\mathcal N_r,1)$ as sharp observables in the sense of clause (c) of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]], with dimensionless particle-count unit. On $\mathcal H$ define
$$\mathcal N_r\psi=\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathcal C}n_r\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle u_{\mathbf n},\qquad D(\mathcal N_r)=\Bigl\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathcal C}n_r^2|\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
To specify the joint occupation readout using a single sharp observable, let $j(\mathbf n)$ be the zero-based position of $\mathbf n$ in the enumeration above (the same ordering on the finite set in the all-F case). Define $J\psi=\sum_{\mathbf n}j(\mathbf n)\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle u_{\mathbf n}$ on $D(J)=\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n}j(\mathbf n)^2|\langle\psi,u_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2<\infty\}$. citations.quote:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statement of isolated autonomous dynamics. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), which are the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral and group suppliers.

**(i) Energy operator.** An **isolated autonomous system** of the sector has a declared **energy operator** $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ that is self-adjoint ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]) and a declared energy unit in which its spectral coordinate is read. The energy operator is part of the model specification of the system; for a massive particle it is fixed by the kinematics postulate P5, and singular or unbounded model Hamiltonians require their own self-adjointness statements.

**(ii) Evolution.** The time evolution of the model is the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad U(t+s)=U(t)U(s),\quad U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1},$$
defined by the spectral calculus of the self-adjoint generator ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]], [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]], [[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The energy unit enters the argument of the exponential so that $H_{\mathrm{op}}t/\hbar$ acts in the dimensionless spectral variable.

**(iii) State evolution.** A vector state evolves continuously, $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the Schroedinger equation
$$i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)=H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(t)$$
holds in the norm-differentiable sense exactly for initial vectors $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, where the derivative is the norm limit of the difference quotients; for other vectors the equation is not asserted, although the evolution remains continuous. A density-operator preparation evolves as $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$, which is a density operator for every $t$ and satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho(t)=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]).

**(iv) Time-dependent families.** A prescribed time-dependent family $t\mapsto H(t)$ of self-adjoint operators is a different model assumption: a norm-continuous finite-dimensional Hermitian family is used only through the unitary two-time propagator that its family defines, and the exponential of the integral of $H(t)$ is not identified with that propagator unless the family commutes with itself at different times. The general unbounded time-dependent case requires a separate existence and domain theorem of its own and is not adopted by this postulate; the driven-dynamics page states its own assumptions for the models it treats.

**(v) Open systems.** A non-unitary evolution of the reduced description of a system coupled to an environment is an extension obtained from an explicitly chosen environment model and a declared reduction, not a replacement for clause (ii); no environment model is adopted by this postulate.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the isolated-system idealization. They assert nothing about the origin of the energy operator of a concrete system, about the accuracy of the idealization for a laboratory preparation, or about which laboratory interactions realize an isolated evolution; those are tested identifications in the sense of P7.

**(a) Assigned energy observable.** Adopt the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4) for a declared isolated system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned energy observable** of the system is an assigned sharp observable $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ in the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), whose declared unit $u_H$ is an energy unit in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] (joules in the SI conventions fixed there). Thus $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ is densely defined and self-adjoint ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), with spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ under the choice hypotheses of [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and its outcome law in a preparation is the law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). The assignment of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is part of the model specification, as in clause (i) of P4; this definition asserts nothing about which laboratory quantity of a concrete system realizes it.

**(b) The unitary flow.** The **time evolution** or **flow** of the isolated system is the family
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. Equivalently, $U(t)=e^{itT}$ for the self-adjoint generator $T:=-H_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ with $D(T)=D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$; the two readings agree by the uniqueness of the generator in Stone's theorem, and by [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]] ([[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-flow-calculus]] clause (a)) the family $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: $U(0)=I$, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, $U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1}=U(-t)$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]).

**(c) Schroedinger picture.** The **Schroedinger-picture evolution** of a preparation is fixed by clause (iii) of P4. A state vector evolves by $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the **state at time $t$** of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ is the pure preparation $[\psi(t)]$, which is well defined because $U(t)$ is injective; a general preparation $\rho$, that is an element of the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], evolves by
$$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$
the reading of clause (iii) of P4 in the density-operator vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). In this picture the assigned observables are held fixed at their assigned values and the preparation moves.

**(d) Heisenberg picture.** For a **bounded** assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ — that is, an assigned sharp observable with $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $A$ is self-adjoint and everywhere defined — the **Heisenberg representative** of $(A,u_A)$ at time $t$ is the pair $(A_H(t),u_A)$ with the same declared unit and
$$A_H(t):=U(t)^{*}AU(t)=U(-t)AU(t).$$
By [[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-heisenberg-flow]] clauses (a) and (d), $A_H(t)$ is again bounded and self-adjoint with spectral projection-valued measure $E_{A_H(t)}(B)=U(-t)E_A(B)U(t)$, so $(A_H(t),u_A)$ is again an assigned sharp observable of the framework; in this picture the preparation is held fixed at its value at time $0$ and the observables move. The two pictures are two bookkeeping devices for the same model; the statement that they assign the same outcome laws is proved in the Heisenberg-picture theorem of this page, not assumed here.

**(e) Stationary preparations.** A preparation $\rho\in D(H)$ is **stationary** for the assigned energy observable when $\rho(t)=\rho$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. A pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary when $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, that is, when the evolved vector remains in the ray of $\psi$; the characterization of this condition by the eigenrays of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is proved in the stationary-states theorem of this page, not assumed here. An **energy eigenstate** is a pure preparation of a unit eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$, and a **stationary state** in the model is a stationary pure preparation; by that theorem the two notions coincide.

**(f) Energy-compatible observables.** An assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ is **compatible with the energy**, or **energy-compatible**, when its spectral projection-valued measure and that of the energy commute strongly,
$$E_A(B)E_H(C)=E_H(C)E_A(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
This is an equality of bounded operators on $H$, not a relation between formal commutators on a small domain; the phrase **conserved quantity** for an energy-compatible assigned observable is a claim about the time invariance of its outcome law and is established in the energy-conservation theorem of this page for bounded $A$.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P4 together with P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P4, P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematics, assert no dynamics for a prescribed time-dependent family or for an open system (clauses (iv) and (v) of P4 are separate model assumptions treated on their own pages), assert no measurement model, no apparatus realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any laboratory system is exactly isolated.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and the canonical Gibbs-preparation assumption [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]]. Restrict to its $G=H$ branch: the declared energy operator $H$ is self-adjoint, bounded below, and measured in joules; $T>0$ is in kelvins, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ is in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, and $K_\beta=e^{-\beta H}$ has $0<Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta<\infty$. Suppose also that on an open interval $J_\beta\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\beta$, every compact $C\subset J_\beta$ admits a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all energy eigenvalues $E_j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Let $(u_j)$ be the finite or countable complete orthonormal eigenfamily supplied by [[thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model]], repeated according to multiplicity, with $Hu_j=E_ju_j$, and put $\lambda_j=e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta$. The supplied trace identity gives $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$, and these $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho_\beta$. The finite canonical, maximum-entropy, independent-factorization and finite-bath claims concern the exact finite state spaces and shell-weight assumptions stated in their items. Countable and measurable derivative identities require their local summable or integrable moment envelopes; a lower energy bound alone does not normalize the partition function. The lattice bulk-pressure and concentration claims apply only to the bounded finite-range lattice model and, for concentration, a differentiability point of the limiting log-partition density. The page-level continuum-pressure prerequisite is a distinct interaction model; no stable-tempered continuum limit is inferred from the lattice theorem.

Regular-shell preparation requires a nonempty compact regular level, the normalized coarea measure, and AC; it does not require a globally defined flow. The separate invariant-shell theorem adds a smooth invertible Hamiltonian flow on the full band, with time in seconds, and proves measure invariance only. Neither result implies ergodicity or equality of long-time averages with the shell law. The quantum Gibbs and finite-mode trace identities explicitly assume AC and Countable Choice, a semibounded self-adjoint generator, a positive finite Gibbs trace and the stated moment envelope. In the general quantum branch, the mean, variance and von Neumann entropy are defined by the supplied Gibbs eigenfamily sums, so no unbounded operator-trace product is being asserted. Discrete dephasing is a trace-norm Cesaro limit with degenerate eigenspaces retained, not pointwise relaxation or a Gibbs limit.

Boltzmann microstate entropy, finite Gibbs entropy, von Neumann entropy and the macroscopic entropy function are distinct objects until a model supplies an explicit identification. The statistical value $-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ is not silently identified with a macroscopic Helmholtz or grand potential. Canonical and microcanonical sampling are adopted preparation assumptions. None of the finite probability identities, continuum or lattice pressure limits, shell-invariance results or quantum trace calculations reports an experiment or establishes that nature follows the model.

Assume AC and Countable Choice and adopt the quantum Gibbs preparation of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]] at assigned temperature $T>0$ kelvins, with $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. A finite independent mode list means an integer $m\ge1$ and, for each $r\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, a declared type B or F and an excitation energy $\varepsilon_r>0$ joules. For type B take the one-mode Fock Hilbert space with complete number basis $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ and self-adjoint occupation operator $N_re_n=ne_n$ on its exact diagonal domain as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-single-mode-thermal-trace]]. For type F take $\mathcal H_r=\mathbb C^2$ with orthonormal basis $f_0,f_1$ and $N_rf_n=nf_n$. In either case put $H_r=\varepsilon_rN_r$, and write $u_{r,n}=e_n$ or $f_n$ according to the factor type. Assign each factor readout $(N_r,1)$ and the composite readout $(\mathcal N_r,1)$ as sharp observables in the sense of clause (c) of [[post-nrqm-many-body-canonical-equilibrium-ensemble]], with dimensionless particle-count unit. On $\mathcal H$ define

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

A finite statistical microstate model is a pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ where $\Omega$ is a finite nonempty set and $\epsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ assigns a finite numerical energy to each microstate. The physical energy of $x\in\Omega$ is $E(x)=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$, with its zero and any retained internal offsets fixed by the declared material model. For a physical internal-energy interpretation, the declared companion mechanical model supplies, for every admitted microstate preparation $x$, a positive total mass and a center-of-mass position map with a defined componentwise velocity at that preparation, obeying the Galilean transformation conditions of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. That velocity selects the statewise instantaneous rest chart in which $E(x)$ is recorded; a finite set and energy map alone do not construct these mechanical data or a common rest chart for a time interval. Bulk translational kinetic energy and separately tracked external-field energy are excluded from these internal-energy values. The energy zero and any internal offsets are fixed consistently across admitted states. If the statistical model also assigns a single equilibrium macrostate to a preparation, $U$ is its internal-energy coordinate of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]; the pair $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ alone does not assert that macroscopic identification. Equal energy values at distinct elements of $\Omega$ count as distinct microstates.

When two such models are declared independent, their joint microstate set is the Cartesian product $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$, and additivity of the microscopic energy is the explicit condition $\epsilon_{AB}(x,y)=\epsilon_A(x)+\epsilon_B(y)$. Independence and this energy equation are model data; they do not follow merely from the two systems being separated. The definition itself assigns no weights, temperature, probability law, or dynamics.

Let $(\Omega,\epsilon)$ be a finite microstate model with energies $E_x=\epsilon(x)\,\mathrm J$ from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]. Let $T>0$, $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$, and $P_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta E_x}/Z(\beta)$ be the adopted preparation of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]]. With $\bar E_\beta=\sum_xP_\beta(x)E_x$, $\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)=\sum_xP_\beta(x)(E_x-\bar E_\beta)^2$, and $S_\beta=-k_{\mathrm B}\sum_xP_\beta(x)\log P_\beta(x)$, the finite partition sum is positive and
$$-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E_\beta,\qquad \partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E),\qquad S_\beta=k_{\mathrm B}(\log Z+\beta\bar E_\beta).$$
Consequently the statistical free-energy value $F_{\mathrm{stat}}:=-k_{\mathrm B}T\log Z$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{stat}}=\bar E_\beta-TS_\beta$. The derivatives hold the finite state set and its energy list fixed. No equivalence with a macroscopic entropy or Helmholtz potential is asserted.

Let two finite microstate models from [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]] have nonempty state sets $\Omega_A,\Omega_B$, energies $E_A,E_B$ in joules, and the same $T>0$. Assume their declared composite model has state set $\Omega_A\times\Omega_B$ and energy $E_{AB}(x,y)=E_A(x)+E_B(y)$, with no interaction term. Under the canonical sampling assumption [[post-td-canonical-sampling]], the partition function factorizes as $Z_{AB}=Z_AZ_B$, the joint canonical law is $P_{AB}=P_AP_B$, the Gibbs entropy satisfies $S_{AB}=S_A+S_B$, and the statistical free-energy value satisfies $F_{AB}=F_A+F_B$.

$$Z(\beta)=\sum_{i\in I}g_i e^{-\beta E_i},\qquad P_\beta(i)=\frac{g_i e^{-\beta E_i}}{Z(\beta)},$$
only at parameters with $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$. Thus the counted-once law is exactly $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$. To match [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]], set $E_*=1\,\mathrm J$, $e_i=E_i/E_*\in\mathbb R$ and $b=E_*\beta$; its real-valued energy and parameter coordinates are $e_i,b$, and its admissible set is $J_Z$ for the declared parameter interval. Its nonnegative sums are suprema of finite subsums. The weights $g_i$ are declared model data, not inferred degeneracies or measurements.

For a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable finite physical energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, adopt the probability density $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$, with $Z(\beta)=\int_X e^{-\beta E}\,d\mu$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$. Measurability of $E$ means measurability of its numerical coordinate $E/E_*$. The integral convention is [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at its current draft definition.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$. A countable probability law on $I$ means a nonnegative family with total sum $1$ under the finite-subsum convention above; these weights form such a law because $\sum_i p_i(\beta)=Z(\beta)/Z(\beta)=1$. For any real family $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

This framework uses the modern International System of Units (SI). A scalar quantity has a real numerical value with the stated unit; a vector quantity has a value in the stated real coordinate space with the stated component unit. The numerical coordinates used elsewhere on this page are divided by their displayed SI units before they are placed in a Euclidean coordinate space.

The model's energy coordinate $U$ and its process-transfer values $Q$ and $W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are scalar energies measured in joules (J). Volume $V$ is a scalar measured in cubic metres (m³); amount of substance $n_j$ for species $j$ is a scalar measured in moles (mol); and a particle count $N_j$, when separately used in a microscopic model, is dimensionless. Time $t$ is measured in seconds (s), mass $M$ in kilograms (kg), and a translational velocity $\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is a vector in $\mathbb R^3$ with components measured in metres per second (m/s). The physical meanings of $U,Q,W_{\mathrm{on}}$ are fixed by the state and process definitions, not by their units alone.

The relevant exact SI relations are

$$1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm N=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}},\qquad 1\,\mathrm{Pa}=1\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$

The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. The Boltzmann constant has the exact defining value $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance; the Avogadro constant has the exact defining value $N_{\mathrm A}=6.02214076\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$. When a model uses particle counts, $n_j=N_j/N_{\mathrm A}$. The molar gas constant is derived as $R=N_{\mathrm A}k_{\mathrm B}=8.31446261815324\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. This framework does not set $k_{\mathrm B}=1$. These SI definitions do not themselves introduce a thermodynamic temperature state function or entropy function.

Within the macroscopic framework, $(U,V,n_j)$ are adopted state coordinates. A quantity's status as primitive in this model is separate from whether its SI unit is a base or derived unit.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

citations.quote: For the finite or explicitly enumerated countable index set $I$ of [[def-tdmath-diagonal-operator-model]], the inner-product space $\ell^2(I)$ is complete and therefore a complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in the first variable. For any real family $(E_i)$, the displayed domain $D(H_E)$ is a linear subspace containing every finite-support vector, is dense in $\ell^2(I)$, and $x\mapsto(E_ix_i)_i$ is a linear map from that domain into $\ell^2(I)$. These assertions also hold for the empty finite index set.

derivations.claim: The trace contribution from states supported on the first $M$ modes is the finite product $Z_M=(1-q)^{-M}$ by [F1]. Since $c=(1-q)^{-1}>1$, $Z_M=c^M$ is unbounded: writing $c=1+r$ with $r>0$, induction gives $(1+r)^M\ge1+Mr$. The unit convention [F5] makes $\beta\varepsilon$ dimensionless.

If $K_\beta$ were trace class, [F3] would make its positive eigenvalue sum finite and equal to its trace. For each $M$, the configurations with $n_j=0$ for $j>M$ form a subset of the enumerated states [A1]; [F4] therefore makes their finite-mode partition sum $Z_M$ no larger than the full normalizer. [F1] identifies that subset sum as $Z_M$, and step 1.1 makes $Z_M$ unbounded, a contradiction. Hence $K_\beta$ is not trace class and the countable partition sum has no finite value. The preparation condition [F2] fails, so this model has no normalized countable canonical law of the stated form.

Assume AC and Countable Choice as required by [[pthm-td-finite-mode-occupation-and-trace-formulas]] and the trace-class suppliers. Take modes indexed by $j\in\mathbb N$, each with excitation energy $\varepsilon>0$ joules, and let $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}\in(0,1)$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the set of finite-support occupation sequences $n=(n_j)_{j\ge1}$ with $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$. Enumerate $\mathcal F$ by increasing $R(n)=\sum_{j:n_j>0}(j+n_j)$ and lexicographic order of the finite list of nonzero pairs $(j,n_j)$ within each level. Each level is finite because $j,n_j\le R(n)$ on its support, and every configuration occurs; skipping empty levels gives a bijection $\mathbb N\to\mathcal F$. Define
$$\ell^2(\mathcal F):=\Bigl\{c:\mathcal F\to\mathbb C:\sum_{n\in\mathcal F}|c(n)|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \langle c,d\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathcal F}c(n)\overline{d(n)}.$$
The vector $|n\rangle$ is the indicator of $\{n\}$; these canonical occupation vectors form an orthonormal basis. Relabeling by the displayed enumeration is an isometry with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb C)$, whose completeness and dense finite-support subspace are supplied by [[lem-tdmath-diagonal-model-hilbert-and-domain]]; the coordinate pairing makes the displayed indicator vectors orthonormal, and their finite linear span is exactly that dense subspace, so they form an orthonormal basis; the definition of square-summable families and their inner product is [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the bounded positive diagonal Gibbs weight $K_\beta|n\rangle=q^{\sum_jn_j}|n\rangle$. On the subspace with $n_j=0$ for every $j>M$, the corresponding finite-mode partition sum is the trace of that restriction.
